body_en: My name is Aziz. I am eleven years old and I live in Tashkent. There are five people in my family: my father, my mother, my two sisters, and me. My father is a doctor. He works at a big hospital. My mother is a teacher. She teaches English at a school near our house. My sisters are students. In the evening we eat dinner together and talk about our day. I love my family very much.
summary_uz: Aziz o'z oilasi haqida gapiradi: otasi shifokor, onasi o'qituvchi, ikki opasi talaba. Kechqurun ular birga ovqatlanishadi.

body_en: On Sunday morning, Dilnoza goes to the market with her grandmother. The market is big and full of people. First, they buy apples and grapes. The fruit is fresh and cheap. Then they buy bread and cheese. Dilnoza's grandmother knows many sellers, and they always smile at her. Before they go home, Dilnoza drinks a cup of tea and eats a hot samsa. She likes Sundays at the market.

My favourite lesson is English because our teacher plays word games with us. At twelve o'clock we have lunch in the school canteen. After school I do my homework, and then I play football with my friends in the yard. I go to bed at ten o'clock.

body_en: Last month, our class travelled to Samarkand by fast train. The journey took about two hours, and we played cards and watched the fields go past the window. In Samarkand we visited Registan Square. Our guide told us that people built these beautiful madrasahs hundreds of years ago. The blue domes shone in the sun, and everyone took photos. At lunchtime we tried Samarkand bread, which is famous all over Uzbekistan. I bought a small painted plate for my mother. On the way home, everybody was tired but happy. I want to go back next year with my family.

I ordered coffee and a piece of honey cake; Malika chose green tea because she doesn't drink coffee in the afternoon. The waiter was friendly and brought our order quickly. The cake was delicious, but the coffee was a little bitter for me. The prices are cheaper than at the old café on the corner. We agreed to come back next week and bring our manager.

body_en: My grandfather has a large garden behind his house in the village. Every spring he plants tomatoes, cucumbers, and peppers, and in summer the whole family helps him water the plants. He wakes up before sunrise because he says the garden is quietest in the early morning. Last year the weather was very dry, and he was worried about his vegetables. Luckily, it rained in July, and the harvest was better than ever. My grandfather always gives boxes of tomatoes to his neighbours. "A good garden makes good friends," he likes to say.

body_en: Five years ago, most students in my town had never taken an online course. Today, almost everyone I know studies something on the internet: languages, programming, design, or even cooking. The main advantage is flexibility — you can watch a lesson at midnight or during your lunch break, and repeat difficult parts as many times as you need. However, online learning also has a serious weakness: without a teacher watching, it is easy to lose motivation. Research suggests that most people who start a free online course never finish it. In my experience, the students who succeed set a fixed time for study, turn off their phone notifications, and find a friend to learn with. Technology gives us the door, but we still have to walk through it ourselves.
summary_uz: Onlayn ta'lim qulay va moslashuvchan, ammo motivatsiyani saqlash qiyin. Muvaffaqiyat qozonganlar aniq jadval tuzadi va do'st bilan birga o'qiydi.

body_en: When Karim turned sixteen, his father gave him an old bicycle instead of the new smartphone he had asked for. At first, Karim was disappointed and left the bicycle in the yard for weeks. One rainy afternoon, bored and offline, he decided to repair it. He cleaned the rusty chain, pumped the tyres, and painted the frame dark green. The work took three weekends, but when he finally rode it through the neighbourhood, he felt strangely proud. Soon he was cycling to school every day, saving the bus money, and exploring streets he had never seen. A year later, Karim told his father the bicycle was the best present he had ever received — not because of what it was, but because of what it had taught him.

body_en: Uzbekistan is a country of sunshine, but that sunshine comes at a price: water is precious here. Farmers in the Aral Sea region remember when the sea reached their villages; today the shore lies many kilometres away. Scientists say that old irrigation methods wasted enormous amounts of water, because open canals lose much of it to the sun before it ever reaches the fields. Modern drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to each plant's roots through thin pipes, can cut water use by more than half. The technology is not cheap, and many small farms cannot afford it without help. Still, every year more fields switch to the new system. Saving water, experts argue, is no longer a choice for the region — it is the only way to keep farming alive for the next generation.

The organiser thanked us and invited us to join another project next month: helping an animal shelter.

body_en: Two years ago, an empty piece of land behind our local clinic was full of rubbish and tall grass. A group of neighbours asked the council if they could turn it into a community garden. The council agreed, but it could not provide money for tools or plants. Instead, residents collected small donations, and a nearby hardware shop gave them seeds at a lower price. Today, the garden has vegetables, herbs, and a small area where children can learn about insects. Each family looks after one part of the garden, but everyone shares the harvest. The project has not solved every problem in the neighbourhood, yet it has created a reason for people of different ages to meet and work together.

body_en: When my aunt started working from home, she imagined that she would have more free time. At first, she enjoyed avoiding the rush-hour bus and making lunch in her own kitchen. However, she soon noticed that her work and home life were mixing together. Because her laptop was always nearby, she often answered messages late at night. She also missed the short conversations with colleagues that used to happen naturally in the office. After a few months, she made three rules: she begins work at the same time every day, takes a real lunch break away from her desk, and closes her laptop when the working day ends. These changes have not made home working perfect, but they have made it more balanced.

body_en: The phrase smart city often brings to mind impressive control rooms, autonomous vehicles, and data flowing through every street. In practice, the most useful changes are frequently less dramatic. A sensor that tells a maintenance team when a public bin is full can prevent overflowing rubbish. A traffic system that adjusts signal timing after an accident may shorten delays for thousands of commuters. These tools can make public services more responsive, but they also raise an important question: who decides which data are collected and how long they are kept? City leaders sometimes present technology as a neutral solution, yet the priorities built into a system reflect human choices. A useful smart-city project should therefore be judged not only by whether it is innovative, but by whether residents can understand, question, and benefit from it.

body_en: For many years, replacing a broken product seemed simpler than repairing it. Low prices, fast delivery, and sealed electronic parts encouraged consumers to treat phones, appliances, and even clothing as temporary possessions. Recently, however, repair has begun to return to public attention. Independent repair shops, community workshops, and online guides give people more ways to extend the life of what they own. Supporters argue that repair saves money, reduces waste, and teaches practical skills. Manufacturers respond that modern devices are complex and that unrestricted repairs can create safety or security risks. The debate is not simply about nostalgia for older products. It is about whether people should have reasonable access to spare parts, clear manuals, and repair information after they have bought an item.

body_en: People often say that learning a new word is like putting a file into a cabinet: once it is stored, it should be available whenever it is needed. Memory does not work so neatly. A word may seem familiar when we see it in a text yet remain difficult to produce in conversation. Researchers distinguish between recognition, which is the ability to identify a word, and recall, which is the ability to retrieve it without a prompt. This difference helps explain why repeated exposure alone is not enough for confident language use. Learners benefit when they meet a word in varied contexts, try to use it themselves, and return to it after a delay. Forgetting is not always a sign of failure; the effort of retrieving partly forgotten information can strengthen the memory trace. Effective revision is therefore less about rereading a long list and more about making recall an active habit.

body_en:
For centuries, a forest was pictured as a loose collection of individual trees, each competing separately for light, water and space. Research over the past three decades has complicated this picture considerably. Beneath the visible canopy, the roots of most forest trees are connected to thread-like fungal filaments known as mycorrhizae, which extend the reach of a root system far beyond what the tree could achieve alone. In exchange for sugars produced through photosynthesis, the fungus supplies the tree with water and mineral nutrients drawn from a much larger volume of soil. Crucially, a single fungal network rarely serves only one tree; instead it often links dozens of trees, sometimes of different species, into a shared underground web.

This network appears to do more than transport nutrients. Some studies suggest that trees connected by the same fungal web can pass warning signals to one another. When a tree is attacked by insects, nearby trees linked through the network sometimes begin producing defensive chemicals before the insects reach them, as though they had been alerted in advance. Older, larger trees — sometimes informally called "hub" trees because of how many smaller trees connect through them — appear to play an outsized role in these exchanges, in some cases channelling surplus sugars toward struggling seedlings growing in their shade. Whether this amounts to genuine cooperation, or is simply an incidental side effect of a system that evolved for other reasons, remains a matter of debate among biologists.

Skeptics of the more dramatic claims point out that a forest is still, in many respects, a competitive environment: trees fight for the same light and the same soil nutrients, and a fungus has its own interests, which do not always align neatly with any single tree's welfare. A fungal network might move resources toward whichever tree offers it the best return, not out of any collective plan. Even so, few researchers now dispute that the network exists and that it measurably affects how trees grow, defend themselves and, at times, die together during drought or disease.

The practical implications of this research are only beginning to be explored. Forestry practices that once focused on planting rows of a single, fast-growing species are being reconsidered in places where mixed, connected stands appear more resilient to pests and changing rainfall patterns. Removing a small number of old hub trees during logging, once considered a minor loss, may in fact disrupt a network that many younger trees depend on. Some conservationists now argue that protecting a handful of the oldest, best-connected trees in a forest could do more for its long-term health than planting a much larger number of new saplings elsewhere.

None of this suggests that trees possess anything like consciousness or intention in the way animals do. But it does suggest that a forest behaves less like a collection of separate individuals and more like a single, loosely coordinated system, in which information as well as nutrients flow along paths that remain, for the most part, hidden beneath the soil.

Eng katta va eski daraxtlar ("hub" daraxtlar) bu tarmoqda alohida muhim rol o'ynaydi, ammo bu haqiqiy hamkorlikmi yoki tasodifiy natijami — olimlar hali bahslashmoqda.

body_en:
Long before modern engineering made large-scale water management routine, several ancient civilisations built cities whose survival depended on an intimate, carefully maintained relationship with water. Three examples — Venice in northern Italy, Angkor in present-day Cambodia, and Tenochtitlan in the Valley of Mexico — illustrate strikingly different solutions to the same underlying challenge: how to make a wet, unstable landscape support a dense urban population.

Venice was built on a cluster of low, marshy islands in a tidal lagoon, a location chosen less for comfort than for safety from raiders who could not easily cross open water. Its builders drove thousands of wooden piles deep into the soft mud beneath the lagoon, creating stable platforms on which stone buildings could stand for centuries. The city's canals were never simply decorative; they functioned as its principal streets, and the rise and fall of the tide helped flush waste out toward the open sea. Maintaining this balance required constant vigilance. Silt carried in by rivers threatened to fill the lagoon and turn it into solid marshland, so authorities diverted several rivers away from the lagoon over the centuries specifically to protect the delicate hydrological balance the city depended on.

Angkor, the capital of the Khmer Empire, faced almost the opposite problem: a climate with a long dry season followed by intense monsoon rains. Its engineers built an immense network of reservoirs, called barays, along with canals and embankments, to capture monsoon water and release it gradually throughout the year. This system supported rice agriculture on a scale sufficient to feed a population that some estimates place in the hundreds of thousands, remarkable for a pre-industrial city. Recent surveys using airborne laser mapping have revealed that Angkor's urban area, once thought to be limited to its famous temple complexes, in fact sprawled across a low-density landscape of canals, ponds and agricultural plots far larger than earlier researchers had assumed. Some historians now believe that gradual damage to this water system, worsened by unusually erratic weather, contributed to the city's eventual decline.

Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, took yet another approach. Founded on an island in Lake Texcoco, the city expanded using chinampas — narrow artificial islands built up from layers of lake mud and vegetation, separated by narrow canals that also served as transport routes. Causeways with removable wooden bridge sections connected the city to the lakeshore, allowing it to be sealed off in times of conflict. To protect the city's freshwater supply from the lake's saltier sections, engineers built a long dike that separated fresh and brackish water, an undertaking that required coordinating labour on a citywide scale.

What unites these three cities is not any single technique but a shared recognition that water could not simply be pushed aside; it had to be actively managed, often at enormous and continuous cost in labour. When that management failed or was abandoned — through conquest, changing climate, or the simple accumulation of small deferred repairs — the consequences for these cities were severe. Their engineering achievements remain a reminder that urban infrastructure is rarely a one-time construction project but an ongoing negotiation with the surrounding environment.

body_en:
For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated by scientists as a passive state, little more than the switching-off of a tired brain. That view has changed substantially. Modern sleep research portrays sleep as an actively managed process, organised into distinct stages that each appear to serve different biological functions, and increasingly linked to outcomes as varied as memory, immune function and emotional regulation.

A typical night's sleep cycles repeatedly through several stages, broadly divided into non-REM and REM (rapid eye movement) sleep. Non-REM sleep itself deepens in stages, culminating in what is often called slow-wave or deep sleep, during which brain activity slows markedly and the body is at its most difficult to wake. REM sleep, by contrast, is associated with vivid dreaming and a pattern of brain activity that in some respects resembles wakefulness, even though the body's major muscles are temporarily paralysed. Each cycle through these stages lasts roughly ninety minutes, and a full night typically includes four to six cycles, with the proportion of deep sleep concentrated earlier in the night and REM sleep becoming more prominent toward morning.

Underlying this nightly pattern is an internal timekeeping system known as the circadian rhythm, a roughly 24-hour cycle generated by a small region of the brain that responds strongly to light. Exposure to daylight, particularly in the morning, helps keep this internal clock aligned with the external day; artificial light in the evening, especially the blue-toned light emitted by many screens, can delay it, pushing the body's natural readiness for sleep later than is convenient for school or work schedules. This mismatch between an individual's internal clock and externally imposed schedules is thought to be widespread, particularly among adolescents, whose circadian rhythms tend to shift later during the teenage years even as school start times remain early.

The consequences of insufficient or poor-quality sleep extend well beyond simple tiredness. During deep sleep, the brain appears to consolidate newly formed memories, transferring information from short-term to more durable long-term storage; students who sleep poorly after studying tend to retain less of what they learned than those who sleep well. Sleep deprivation has also been linked to impaired judgement and slower reaction times, effects that in some studies were comparable to those caused by alcohol consumption. Longer-term, chronic short sleep has been associated with increased risk of several health conditions, including weakened immune response and disruptions to the hormones that regulate appetite, which may partly explain observed links between poor sleep and weight gain.

Despite this growing body of evidence, sleep remains, in many societies, treated as a flexible resource to be reduced whenever other demands increase — a reputation reinforced by cultures that praise long working hours over adequate rest. Sleep researchers increasingly argue that this attitude misunderstands what sleep actually does: not a period of inactivity to be minimised, but an active process on which many other functions, from learning to physical health, quietly depend.

A century ago, most people on Earth could step outside after dark and see thousands of stars, along with the faint band of the Milky Way stretching across the sky. Today, largely because of artificial lighting, a majority of the world's population lives under skies bright enough to hide all but the brightest stars. This phenomenon, known as light pollution, has quietly become one of the most widespread forms of environmental change on the planet, yet it receives far less public attention than pollution of air or water.

Light pollution takes several forms. Skyglow is the diffuse brightening of the night sky caused by artificial light scattering off particles and moisture in the atmosphere, and it can be seen from many kilometres beyond a city's edge. Glare from poorly shielded lights can be dangerous as well as unpleasant, temporarily reducing a driver's ability to see the road. Light trespass occurs when light spills beyond the area it is meant to illuminate, for instance into a neighbour's bedroom window. Unlike many pollutants, artificial light at night does not accumulate or persist once its source is switched off, which means that, in principle, light pollution is one of the more immediately reversible forms of environmental damage.

The ecological consequences of constant artificial light are increasingly well documented. Sea turtle hatchlings, which instinctively move toward the brightest visible horizon after emerging from their nests, can be fatally misled by coastal lighting away from the sea. Migratory birds that navigate partly by starlight can become disoriented around brightly lit buildings, sometimes colliding with windows in large numbers during migration season. Many nocturnal insects are drawn to artificial lights and can die from exhaustion or predation as a result, a pattern some researchers believe is contributing to broader declines in insect populations, with knock-on effects for the birds and other animals that depend on insects for food. Even some trees have shown altered seasonal patterns of budding and leaf loss when situated near strong artificial lighting.

The response to these findings has grown into an international movement, loosely organised around the idea of "dark sky" preservation. Certified dark sky parks and reserves now exist on several continents, protected through a combination of shielded lighting, reduced brightness, and warmer-toned bulbs that scatter less strongly into the atmosphere than the harsh blue-white light common in older streetlamps. Some cities have experimented with reducing street lighting after midnight in low-traffic areas, or dimming lights automatically when no pedestrians or vehicles are detected. Advocates argue that most everyday lighting could be made both more effective and less wasteful simply by directing it downward, toward the surfaces people actually need illuminated, rather than allowing it to spread sideways and upward into the sky.

Unlike climate change or plastic pollution, addressing light pollution requires no new technology and comparatively modest investment; much of the necessary equipment, from shielded fixtures to timers and dimmers, is already inexpensive and widely available. What has been missing, dark sky advocates suggest, is not capability but awareness: many people have simply never seen a truly dark sky and so do not recognise what has been lost. For a growing number of astronomers, ecologists and residents of over-lit cities, restoring at least some darkness to the night is now considered not a return to the past but a practical and achievable form of environmental repair.
